verses.text: Manasseh was twelve when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for fifty-five years.
He did evil right in the LORD’s sight, picking up the disgusting practices of the nations the LORD had driven out ahead of the Israelites.
He put back the high places his father Hezekiah had torn down, built altars for the Baals, and made Asherah idols. He bowed down to the whole host of heaven and served them.
He even built altars inside the LORD’s house, the very place the LORD spoke of when he said, “My name will be in Jerusalem forever.”
In both courtyards of the LORD’s house, he set up altars for the whole host of heaven.

He put his own children through the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom. He practiced sorcery, divination, and witchcraft, and went to mediums and wizards. He did so much evil in the LORD’s sight that he provoked him to anger.

He put the idol he’d carved right inside God’s house. God had told David and his son Solomon, “I chose Jerusalem out of all the tribes of Israel. My name will be here in this house and in this city forever.

I won’t make Israel leave the land I set aside for your ancestors again, as long as they pay close attention to everything I commanded them and follow the whole law, the statutes, and the rulings I gave through Moses.”
Manasseh led Judah and the people of Jerusalem so far off course that they did even worse than the nations the LORD had destroyed ahead of the Israelites.
The LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they wouldn’t listen.
So the LORD sent the Assyrian king’s army commanders against them. They captured Manasseh, put him in chains and shackles, and took him to Babylon.
In his trouble, Manasseh begged the LORD his God for help. He humbled himself deeply before the God of his ancestors.
He prayed, and God was moved by his plea. God heard him and brought him back to Jerusalem to rule his kingdom again. Then Manasseh knew the LORD was God.

After that, he built an outer wall for David’s city, west of Gihon in the valley, as far as the entrance at the Fish Gate. He took the wall around Ophel and built it up high. He stationed strong military commanders in every fortified city in Judah.

He got rid of the foreign gods and the idol he’d put in the LORD’s house. He took all the altars he’d built on the hill where the LORD’s house stood and around Jerusalem and threw them outside the city.
He rebuilt the LORD’s altar and offered peace offerings and thank offerings on it. Then he told Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel.
People still made sacrifices at the high places, but they made them only to the LORD their God.
The rest of what Manasseh did, his prayer to his God, and what the seers told him in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel, are written in the records of Israel’s kings.

His prayer and how God heard him are written in the history of Hozai, along with his sin and wrongdoing and the places where he built high places and put up Asherah poles and carved idols before he humbled himself.
Manasseh died and joined his ancestors. They buried him in his own house, and his son Amon became king in his place.
Amon was twenty-two when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for two years.
Like his father Manasseh, Amon did evil in the LORD’s sight. He sacrificed to all the idols his father Manasseh had carved and served them.
Manasseh had humbled himself before the LORD. Amon never did. He just kept piling up more wrongdoing.
His own servants plotted against him and killed him right in his house.
The people of the land killed everyone who’d plotted against King Amon. Then they made his son Josiah king in his place.
